blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The Kaplan–Meier (product-limit) estimate of the survival function is

S(t) = Π over event times tⱼ ≤ t of (1 − dⱼ/nⱼ),

where dⱼ is the number of events at time tⱼ and nⱼ the number at risk just before tⱼ. Plotted against time, it is a step function that starts at 1 and drops only at event times.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The curve is built one event time at a time. At each, ask: of the nⱼ still at risk, what fraction got through? Multiply these fractions together. A censored subject never causes a step. They simply leave the at-risk set, so later fractions have a smaller denominator. This is the mechanism that lets censored subjects count up to their last contact and no further.

The demographic life table does the same job for a population (recall §7.5, where lₓ₊ₙ = lₓ × (1 − ₙqₓ)). Kaplan–Meier builds the survival curve from individual follow-up times instead of age bands.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
To be event-free beyond tⱼ you must be event-free beyond tⱼ₋₁ and then get past tⱼ. By the multiplication rule for conditional probability (recall §5.3):

P(T > tⱼ) = P(T > tⱼ₋₁) × P(T > tⱼ | T > tⱼ₋₁).

The conditional factor is estimated by the fraction of the at-risk set that did not have the event: (nⱼ − dⱼ)/nⱼ = 1 − dⱼ/nⱼ. Between event times nobody has the event, so the factor is 1 and the curve stays flat. Chaining the factors from the start gives the product.

Greenwood’s standard error. Write log S(t) = Σ log(1 − qⱼ), with qⱼ = dⱼ/nⱼ, a proportion out of nⱼ with variance qⱼ(1 − qⱼ)/nⱼ. The delta method (a first-order Taylor approximation, Var[g(X)] ≈ g′(μ)² Var(X), where g′ is the slope, or derivative, of g; the calculus is beyond this book) gives Var[log(1 − qⱼ)] ≈ qⱼ/[nⱼ(1 − qⱼ)] = dⱼ/[nⱼ(nⱼ − dⱼ)]. Adding the terms, and applying the delta method once more to go from log S to S:

Var[S(t)] ≈ S(t)² × Σ dⱼ/[nⱼ(nⱼ − dⱼ)].

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
data/km_eight.csv holds eight CBHI members (months to dropout; + = censored): 2, 4, 4+, 6, 7+, 9, 11, 12+.

Month tⱼ At risk nⱼ Dropouts dⱼ Censored after tⱼ 1 − dⱼ/nⱼ S(tⱼ) Σ dⱼ/[nⱼ(nⱼ − dⱼ)] SE of S(tⱼ)
2 8 1 0 7/8 = 0.875 0.875 0.0179 0.117
4 7 1 1 (4+) 6/7 = 0.857 0.750 0.0417 0.153
6 5 1 1 (7+) 4/5 = 0.800 0.600 0.0917 0.182
9 3 1 0 2/3 = 0.667 0.400 0.2583 0.203
11 2 1 1 (12+) 1/2 = 0.500 0.200 0.7583 0.174
  1. Month 2: all 8 at risk, 1 drops out. S = 7/8 = 0.875.
  2. Month 4: 7 at risk (the tie 4 and 4+ is broken the usual way: the censored member counts as at risk at 4). S = 0.875 × 6/7 = 0.750. Member M3 (4+) then leaves.
  3. Month 6: 5 at risk. S = 0.750 × 4/5 = 0.600. M5 is censored at 7 and leaves without a step.
  4. Month 9: 3 at risk. S = 0.600 × 2/3 = 0.400. Month 11: S = 0.400 × 1/2 = 0.200. The curve stays at 0.200 to 12 months, when the last member is censored.
  5. Greenwood at 9 months: 1/(8 × 7) + 1/(7 × 6) + 1/(5 × 4) + 1/(3 × 2) = 0.0179 + 0.0238 + 0.0500 + 0.1667 = 0.2583. SE = 0.400 × √0.2583 = 0.400 × 0.508 = 0.203. A plain 95% CI, 0.400 ± 1.96 × 0.203, runs from 0.002 to 0.798. With eight members it is wide, and near 0 or 1 a plain interval can cross the limits; software therefore builds the interval on the log or log(−log) scale and back-transforms it.
  6. Median survival is the first time S(t) falls to 0.5 or below. S is 0.600 up to 9 months and 0.400 from 9 months, so the median is 9 months.

If the curve never falls to 0.5 within follow-up, the median is not reached. Report it as “NR” and give S(t) at fixed times instead. Never read a median off an extrapolated curve.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the §14.7 cohort of 300 CBHI households followed for up to 24 months, 120 dropped out, 18 moved away and 162 were still enrolled at 24 months. The Kaplan–Meier retention is S(12) = 0.75 and S(24) = 0.58 (Figure 14.2b). The curve never reaches 0.5, so the median time to dropout is not reached: more than half the households were still enrolled when follow-up ended. The summary is “median NR; 58% still enrolled at 24 months”.

blocks.alt: Kaplan-Meier curves: eight members and the CBHI cohort
blocks.caption: Figure 14.2. (a) The eight-member table above: steps at each dropout, ticks at censored times, median 9 months. (b) The 300-household cohort: short ticks are the 18 households that moved away; the thick tick at 24 months stands for the 162 still enrolled. The curve ends at 0.58, so the median is not reached.

blocks.html:
The actuarial (clinical life-table) method. Before computers, follow-up was grouped into fixed intervals, as in the demographic life table (§7.5). Within each interval, the number at risk is adjusted as n′ = n − w/2, where w is the number withdrawn (censored) in the interval: censored subjects contribute “half to the number of patients at risk” (Held et al., 2026), on the assumption that they left, on average, halfway through. The interval’s probability of the event is q = d/n′, and survival is the running product of (1 − q).

Interval (months) At start n Dropouts d Withdrawn w n′ = n − w/2 q = d/n′ 1 − q S at end
0–3 8 1 0 8.0 0.125 0.875 0.875
3–6 7 1 1 6.5 0.154 0.846 0.740
6–9 5 1 1 4.5 0.222 0.778 0.576
9–12 3 2 0 3.0 0.667 0.333 0.192

Kaplan–Meier gives 0.750, 0.600 and 0.200 just before 6, 9 and 12 months; the actuarial table gives 0.740, 0.576 and 0.192. The actuarial values are slightly lower because each withdrawal is counted as only half at risk. Kaplan–Meier uses exact times and needs no assumption about when within an interval people left. The actuarial method suits large cohorts recorded only by interval, such as routine programme registers.

Surv(time, event) pairs each time with its event indicator. For the eight members, n.risk, survival and std.err reproduce the hand table (8, 7, 5, 3, 2; 0.875 to 0.200; Greenwood SE 0.203 at 9 months), and the median is 9. The confidence limits differ from the plain ones because R builds them on the log scale. For the cohort, n.event counts dropouts since the previous listed time (74 by 12 months, 46 more by 24); S(12) = 0.75 and S(24) = 0.58; and median is NA, R’s way of saying not reached.

points.html: S(t) = Π(1 − dⱼ/nⱼ). The curve is a step function, flat between events.
Censored subjects leave the at-risk set without causing a step. Show them as tick marks on the curve.
The median is the first time S(t) ≤ 0.5. If the curve stays above 0.5, the median is not reached (NR); report S(t) at stated times instead.
The estimate is unreliable in the tail, where few remain at risk. Greenwood SEs widen there (0.203 at 9 months with 3 at risk); a common practice is to show the number at risk beneath the plot.
Actuarial method: fixed intervals, withdrawals count as half at risk. Kaplan–Meier: exact event times.

questions.prompt: In a cohort, S(t) just before month 12 is 0.80. At month 12, 70 members are at risk and 3 drop out. What is S(12)? Is the hazard in that month 3/70 or 3/100 of the original cohort, and why?
questions.answer: S(12) = 0.80 × (1 − 3/70) = 0.80 × 67/70 = 0.80 × 0.957 = 0.766. The month’s hazard is estimated as 3/70 = 0.043 per member-month, because only the 70 still enrolled and under observation could drop out that month. Members who had already dropped out or been censored are no longer in the at-risk set, so dividing by the original 100 would understate the rate.

questions.prompt: In a two-year follow-up of TB patients, the Kaplan–Meier curve ends at 0.64. A colleague reports “median survival 24 months”. What should be reported instead?
questions.answer: The curve never falls to 0.5, so the median is not reached. Report “median NR” and give survival at stated times, e.g. “64% surviving at 24 months” (with its CI). Twenty-four months is simply the end of follow-up, not a median.

questions.prompt: Why is a member who moves away at month 5 not simply deleted from a Kaplan–Meier analysis, and what assumption makes it safe to treat them as censored?
questions.answer: They were known to be enrolled and event-free for 5 months, and that is real information: they count in the at-risk set, in every denominator, up to month 5. Deleting them would discard it and bias the sample towards those with complete follow-up. Treating them as censored is valid under non-informative censoring: households lost to follow-up are assumed as likely to drop out later as similar households that remained under observation. (If moving away itself ended membership, it would be a competing event, §14.8.)
